summary: Specifies the packetization scheme for carrying compressed DV video in RTP. It was replaced by RFC 6469.

eli5.summary: It cuts a home-video stream into packages that can be mailed over the Internet.

questions: rtp payload format for dv video
how does dv work over rtp
dv over rtp bundled vs unbundled
subtitle: A way to send DV video over the internet in real time.

tldr.problem: DV is a compressed video format designed for tape, but people want to send it over the internet in real time without having to decompress and recompress it.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to break DV frames into standardized 80-byte chunks called DIF blocks and pack them into RTP packets, with optional audio bundled alongside.
tldr.outcome: DV video and audio can travel over IP networks. This specification was replaced by RFC 6469.

today: RFC 3189 was obsoleted by RFC 6469 in 2011, which revised the RTP payload format for DV.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DV is a video compression format originally designed for helical-scan magnetic tape in consumer and professional video cameras. The consumer standard is defined by IEC 61834, while professional versions are the SMPTE 306M and 314M standards. This RFC specifies how to send DV video streams across networks using the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP).

DV was designed to compress both video and audio together on tape, with support for multiple video formats (525/60 NTSC and 625/50 PAL variants) and both standard and high definition. The RFC supports all these variants when transmitting over RTP.
sections.eli5: DV is how video cameras compress movies onto tape. This RFC says how to send that same compressed format over the internet instead of tape.

sections.title: DV Format Structure
sections.content:
DV uses DCT (Discrete Cosine Transform) compression applied within each frame independently, rather than compression across frames like MPEG does. A frame of DV data is divided into DIF sequences, which are collections of DIF blocks, each exactly 80 bytes. DIF blocks are the basic unit for all DV stream handling.

Five types of DIF blocks exist: sequence headers (which carry frame metadata), subcode (which carries timecode and other system information), VAUX (video auxiliary data), audio blocks, and video blocks. Audio data is encoded as PCM with a sample rate of 32 kHz, 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz, and either 12-bit non-linear or 16-bit/20-bit linear quantization, with support for up to 8 audio channels.
sections.eli5: DV breaks a video frame into equal-sized 80-byte chunks called DIF blocks. Some blocks carry video, some carry audio, and some carry instructions about how to play it all back.

sections.title: RTP Payload and Encapsulation
sections.content:
RTP packets carrying DV data place whole DIF blocks immediately after the RTP header with no additional payload-specific header. All DIF blocks in a single RTP packet must come from the same video frame; blocks from different frames cannot be mixed in one packet, because frame boundaries are marked by timestamp changes.

The RTP timestamp is based on a 90 kHz clock and represents the time when the first data in the frame was sampled. For different video formats, one frame's timestamp increases by different amounts: NTSC formats (525/60) increase by 3003, PAL formats (625/50) increase by 3600, HD 1125/60 increases by 3000, and HD 1250/50 increases by 3600. The marker bit (M) in the RTP header is set to 1 on the last packet of a video frame and 0 otherwise, allowing receivers to detect frame completion.
sections.eli5: RTP packets just glue the DIF blocks together. Each packet has a timestamp that says when the video frame was recorded, and a flag on the last packet of each frame so the receiver knows when to display the picture.

sections.title: Bundled and Unbundled Streams
sections.content:
DV can be transmitted two ways: bundled, where audio and video blocks travel together in the same RTP stream, or unbundled, where video and audio are sent as separate RTP streams to separate ports or multicast groups. The choice must be made when the dynamic payload type is assigned and cannot change during the session.

In unbundled mode, the video stream carries only header, subcode, video and VAUX blocks; audio blocks are omitted. If audio is needed, it can be extracted from the DV blocks and repacked into a standard audio RTP format (like L16 or L20) for better interoperability with non-DV receivers. For lip synchronization, audio and video timestamps within the same frame should match when unbundled.

DV includes metadata like aspect ratio and audio channel information in source packs within VAUX and audio blocks. Rather than defining extensive Session Description Protocol parameters, senders must transmit at least one set of these source and source control packs so receivers can decode the stream correctly.
sections.eli5: Video and audio can travel together or separately. If separate, the audio can be converted to a simpler format that more devices understand. Either way, the receiver needs to know a few details from the sender about aspect ratio and audio channels.

sections.title: Signaling with SDP
sections.content:
Session Description Protocol (SDP) is used to negotiate RTP streams. For DV over RTP, an SDP media line looks like m=video 31394 RTP/AVP 111, where 111 is the dynamic payload type. The corresponding rtpmap attribute is a=rtpmap:111 DV/90000, where DV is the encoding name and 90000 is the 90 kHz timestamp rate.

Format-specific parameters are supplied via the a=fmtp line. The encode parameter specifies which DV format: one of SD-VCR/525-60, SD-VCR/625-50, HD-VCR/1125-60, HD-VCR/1250-50, SDL-VCR/525-60, SDL-VCR/625-50, 306M, 314M-25, or 314M-50 formats with their /525-60 or /625-50 variants. The optional audio parameter is either bundled or none (the default). Two MIME types are registered: video/DV and audio/DV.
sections.eli5: Before sending DV, the sender and receiver exchange a message that says what kind of video format it is (NTSC or PAL, standard or HD) and whether audio travels with video or separately.
